title: Is Pluto a Planet? What's a Planet, Anyway?

contentUnits.title: Pluto Starts as a Feeling
contentUnits.text:
This debate about the icy world that used to be the ninth planet of the solar system is as much linguistics as science, and it is not a question with simple answers.

But it is a fascinating story about an ancient word with shifting meanings, humanity’s evolving views of its place in the cosmos and the process of scientific discovery, which like all human endeavors, can be messy and contentious.

Are you open to changing your mind about Pluto? Let’s ask a few questions to see where you stand on this question of planetary importance.

lifecycle.transition: Pluto enlarges at center while the other bodies remain dim reference points.
lifecycle.readerAction: Advance after reading the Pluto poll and looking at the centered model.

contentUnits.title: Eris Makes Sentiment Harder
contentUnits.text: But “Is Pluto a planet?” is the wrong question. Or at least, it’s not the only question. Consider these other places in the solar system.

lifecycle.transition: Eris slides beside Pluto at nearly the same scale.
lifecycle.readerAction: Compare Pluto and Eris side by side before advancing.

contentUnits.title: Ceres Shows Categories Can Change
contentUnits.text: Ceres, like Pluto, is a former planet. The question shifts from one favorite object to a history of names, lists and minimum thresholds.

lifecycle.transition: Ceres moves forward and Vesta appears as a smaller lumpy boundary case.
lifecycle.readerAction: Look from Ceres to Vesta to see the size and roundness boundary become less clean.

contentUnits.title: The Moon Tests the Orbit Rule
contentUnits.text: The Moon is round and larger than Pluto, but it orbits Earth. This makes the definition depend on what a body does, not just what it is.

lifecycle.transition: The Moon gets an orbit ring while Pluto remains visible for scale comparison.
lifecycle.readerAction: Use the orbit ring to compare a direct solar planet definition with a geophysical one.

contentUnits.title: Your Answers Pick a Taxonomy
contentUnits.text: Based on the four source questions, the story maps readers into competing definitions: traditional eight, Pluto sentimentalist, a ten-planet compromise, Team Round or a fallback mixed view.

lifecycle.transition: All bodies align on a shared comparison rail.
lifecycle.readerAction: Read the outcome summaries in the data drawer or continue to the definition dispute.

contentUnits.title: What Makes a Planet a Planet?
contentUnits.text:
Why it’s so hard to define “planet”

The crux of the dispute: What makes a planet a planet?
Should a planet be defined by what it is — some specification of size or composition or shape? Or should it be defined by what it does — that it goes around the sun?

Or both?

The word “planet” derives from the Greek word for “wanderer.” To the ancients, the Earth seemed to be the obvious unmoving center of the universe.

Stars seemed to be fixed points of light on a distant rotating globe, but a few brighter spots stood out against the cosmic background. These were Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The moon and the sun were originally counted as planets because, although they were immensely larger, they also wandered across the sky.

lifecycle.transition: Bodies sort between two labeled rails without moving the reader.
lifecycle.readerAction: Compare the two rails: orbit dominance and round-world geology.

contentUnits.title: The Definition Is Still Open
contentUnits.text:
Final thoughts

Science is not a popularity contest. It can be complicated, and scientists do not always agree. But within the differences of opinion often lie intriguing nuances of knowledge.

pluto.prompt: Do you think Pluto should be considered a planet?

eris.prompt: Do you think Eris is a planet?

ceres.prompt: What about Ceres? Should Ceres be a planet?

answers.label: I have never heard of this place. (Wasn’t Ceres the three-headed dog guarding the gates to the Underworld?)

moon.prompt: Last question. Should Earth’s moon be called a planet too?

answers.label: Sure, why not? It’s round. It’s bigger than Pluto.
No! What part of “moon” do you not understand?

final.prompt: Which definition of planets do you prefer now?

answers.label: The current definition. (But leave space for Planet Nine!)
Everything round that directly orbits the sun.
Everything round including the large moons.
We should just retire the word “planet.”
